items.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules across the flexor surfaces of both wrists and volar forearms. Examination of the oral cavity reveals asymptomatic, fine, lacy white reticular lines on the bilateral buccal mucosa. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Lichen planus is classically characterized by the 'six Ps': pruritic, planar, polygonal, purple (violaceous), papules, and plaques, with strong predilection for the flexor wrists and ankles. Wickham striae (lacy white reticular networks) on the buccal mucosa are pathognomonic.
r: Correct: Polygonal violaceous pruritic papules on flexor wrists with oral Wickham striae define lichen planus.
Psoriasis vulgaris features thick silvery scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and lacks oral lacy white striae.
Secondary syphilis produces non-pruritic coppery maculopapules on palms and soles with constitutional symptoms.
Scabies causes intense nocturnal itch with linear burrows in web spaces and inflammatory papules.
items.kp: Lichen planus is characterized by pruritic, polygonal, violaceous papules on flexor surfaces and oral Wickham striae.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for the management of lichen planus

x.key: Violaceous polygonal papules on flexor wrists with oral Wickham striae indicate lichen planus.
x.pearl: First-line treatment for localized cutaneous lichen planus is a potent topical corticosteroid ointment.
x.clues: Flexor wrists, itchy polygonal violaceous papules, lacy white lines on buccal mucosa.
x.ddx: Lichenoid drug eruption, psoriasis, graft-versus-host disease, lupus erythematosus.
x.mech: Cytotoxic CD8+ T-lymphocytes target self-peptides on basal keratinocytes, inducing interface vacuolar degeneration.
x.lo: Recognise the clinical morphology and oral findings of lichen planus.
x.rev: Lichen planus presents with violaceous polygonal pruritic papules and oral Wickham striae.

next.text: Review BAD guidelines on lichen planus.

items.q: A 24-year-old student presents with a solitary 3.5 cm oval, salmon-pink scaly patch on her lower abdomen. Twelve days later, she develops multiple smaller oval scaly maculopapules across her chest and back, arranged symmetrically with their long axes parallel to skin tension lines in a 'Christmas tree' distribution. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Pityriasis rosea characteristically begins with a solitary primary 'herald patch' (2-5 cm oval plaque with a collarette of scale), followed 1-2 weeks later by a secondary eruption of smaller oval lesions aligned along Langer cleavage lines in a 'Christmas tree' pattern on the trunk.
r: Correct: Solitary herald patch followed by Christmas tree trunk eruption defines pityriasis rosea.
Guttate psoriasis lacks a preceding herald patch and presents as small droplet papules following streptococcal pharyngitis.
Tinea versicolor causes asymptomatic coalescent macules without a herald patch or cleavage line pattern.
Secondary syphilis produces generalized non-pruritic papules involving the palms and soles with lymphadenopathy.
items.kp: Pityriasis rosea begins with a solitary herald patch followed by a Christmas tree distribution along skin cleavage lines.
items.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Pityriasis rosea

x.key: Solitary herald patch followed by Christmas tree trunk rash defines pityriasis rosea.

others.B: Guttate psoriasis follows strep throat and lacks a herald patch.

x.pearl: The scale in pityriasis rosea forms a delicate 'collarette' just inside the outer margin of the plaque, facing inward.
x.clues: Primary solitary plaque on abdomen, secondary smaller lesions along cleavage lines in Christmas tree pattern.
x.ddx: Secondary syphilis, guttate psoriasis, tinea corporis, nummular eczema.
x.mech: Associated with endogenous reactivation of human herpesviruses 6 and 7 (HHV-6 / HHV-7).
x.lo: Recognise the presentation and rash distribution of pityriasis rosea.
x.rev: Pityriasis rosea features an initial herald patch followed by a Christmas tree eruption along skin tension lines.

next.text: Review NICE CKS on pityriasis rosea.

items.q: A clinician examines the violaceous polygonal papules on the wrist of a patient suspected of having lichen planus. Applying a drop of mineral oil and examining under dermoscopy reveals fine white reticular striae criss-crossing the surface of the lesions. What is the eponym for these white striae?
items.exp: Wickham striae are fine, white or greyish reticulated lines, dots, or networks visible on the surface of cutaneous papules and oral lesions in lichen planus. Histopathologically, they correspond to focal hypergranulosis of the epidermis.
r: Correct: Fine white reticulated lines in lichen planus are Wickham striae.
Gottron papules are violaceous flat-topped papules over knuckles in dermatomyositis.
Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding after scraping scales off psoriasis plaques.
Asboe-Hansen refers to bulla spread upon vertical pressure in pemphigus.
items.kp: Wickham striae are fine white reticular lines characteristic of lichen planus, corresponding to focal hypergranulosis.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for the management of lichen planus

x.key: Wickham striae are fine white reticular lines seen on lichen planus lesions.
x.pearl: Wickham striae are most readily identified on the buccal mucosa and under oil immersion or dermoscopy on cutaneous papules.
x.clues: Violaceous wrist papules, fine white reticular lines on surface under dermoscopy.
x.ddx: Oral candidiasis, leukoplakia, lichenoid drug eruption.
x.mech: Focal thickening of the stratum granulosum (focal hypergranulosis) scatters light to produce white reticular lines.
x.lo: Identify Wickham striae as a pathognomonic physical finding in lichen planus.
x.rev: Wickham striae are fine white reticular networks characteristic of lichen planus.

next.text: Review physical examination signs in lichen planus.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with persistent, painful, erosive ulcerations on the buccal mucosa surrounded by fine white lacy reticulations. A 4 mm punch biopsy is taken from the margin. What histopathological triad is characteristic of lichen planus?
o: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, basal cell liquefactive degeneration, and apoptotic Civatte bodies
Thickened parakeratotic stratum corneum, microabscesses of Munro, and elongated rete ridges
Intraepidermal suprabasal acantholysis with tombstone basal cells
Subepidermal blister with linear IgG deposition along basement membrane
items.exp: The classic histopathology of lichen planus comprises a dense band-like ('lichenoid') T-lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermo-epidermal junction, basal vacuolar degeneration, apoptotic dyskeratotic keratinocytes (Civatte / colloid bodies), and irregular 'saw-toothed' acanthosis.
r: Correct: Band-like junctional lymphocytic infiltrate with basal vacuolation and Civatte bodies defines lichen planus.
Munro microabscesses, parakeratosis, and regular elongated rete ridges are diagnostic of psoriasis.
Intraepidermal suprabasal acantholysis with tombstone basal cells characterizes pemphigus vulgaris.
Subepidermal blister with linear IgG deposition defines bullous pemphigoid.
items.kp: Lichen planus histopathology shows a band-like junctional lymphocytic infiltrate, basal layer degeneration, and apoptotic Civatte bodies.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for lichen planus

x.key: Band-like junctional lymphocytic infiltrate with Civatte bodies is pathognomonic for lichen planus.

others.B: Munro abscesses and elongated rete pegs are psoriasis.

x.pearl: Civatte bodies (also called colloid or cytoid bodies) represent apoptotic basal keratinocytes that have undergone anucleate degeneration.
x.clues: Painful buccal erosion, white striae, punch biopsy features.
x.ddx: Oral candidiasis, pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, lupus erythematosus.
x.mech: Cytotoxic T-cells release perforin and granzyme B, inducing apoptotic cell death of basal keratinocytes.
x.lo: Describe the characteristic histopathological features of lichen planus.
x.rev: Lichen planus shows a band-like junctional infiltrate, basal liquefaction, and Civatte bodies.

items.q: A 21-year-old university student is diagnosed with pityriasis rosea after presenting with a herald patch and a classical trunk eruption. She is very distressed about the appearance and asks what treatment is needed and when the rash will resolve. In accordance with NICE CKS, what is the appropriate management advice?
o: Reassurance that the rash is benign and resolves spontaneously in 6-8 weeks; prescribe emollients or mild topical steroids if itchy
Immediate oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 14 days
Oral systemic prednisolone 40 mg daily for 4 weeks
Narrowband UVB phototherapy 3 times weekly for 12 weeks
items.exp: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries recommend reassurance as the cornerstone of management: pityriasis rosea is a benign, non-contagious condition that resolves spontaneously within 6 to 12 weeks without scarring. Symptomatic pruritus is managed with emollients, mild topical corticosteroids, or oral antihistamines.
r: Correct: Reassurance of spontaneous resolution in 6-8 weeks with symptomatic emollient/steroid therapy is appropriate.
Routine oral aciclovir is not recommended in standard practice for uncomplicated pityriasis rosea.
Systemic corticosteroids are unnecessary for this self-limiting condition and carry systemic adverse risks.
Routine phototherapy is not indicated for standard uncomplicated pityriasis rosea.
items.kp: Pityriasis rosea is a benign self-limiting condition that resolves in 6-8 weeks; management is reassurance and symptomatic itch relief.
items.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Pityriasis rosea

x.key: Pityriasis rosea resolves spontaneously in 6-8 weeks; treatment is reassurance and symptomatic care.
x.pearl: Patients should be reassured that pityriasis rosea does not leave permanent scars, though post-inflammatory pigmentation may take months to fade.
x.clues: Student with confirmed pityriasis rosea, natural history and management strategy.
x.ddx: Secondary syphilis, gutatte psoriasis, nummular eczema, pityriasis versicolor.
x.mech: Immune clearance of HHV-6/7 leads to spontaneous resolution of the inflammatory exanthem.
x.lo: Advise patients on the natural history and management of pityriasis rosea.
x.rev: Pityriasis rosea resolves spontaneously in 6-8 weeks; manage with reassurance and emollients.

next.text: Review NICE CKS on pityriasis rosea.

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with extensive cutaneous and oral lichen planus. He has no other medical complaints but routine screening reveals mildly elevated liver enzymes. Which chronic viral infection has a well-established epidemiological association with lichen planus and should be screened?
items.exp: A well-established epidemiological association exists between lichen planus (especially erosive and oral variants) and chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The British Association of Dermatologists recommends HCV serology in patients presenting with extensive, erosive, or refractory lichen planus.
r: Correct: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is strongly associated with lichen planus and should be screened.
Hepatitis A is an acute enterically transmitted infection without chronic dermatological sequelae.
EBV causes infectious mononucleosis and lymphomas, not lichen planus.
HPV 16 causes anogenital warts and cervical dysplasia, not lichen planus.
items.kp: Chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is strongly associated with lichen planus.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for the management of lichen planus

x.key: Hepatitis C virus is strongly linked to lichen planus and should be tested.

others.B: HAV is acute and not associated.

x.pearl: The prevalence of HCV antibodies among patients with lichen planus is reported to be between 2% and 10% in Western countries and up to 30% in Mediterranean cohorts.
x.clues: Lichen planus, elevated liver enzymes, associated chronic viral infection.
x.ddx: Hepatitis B, autoimmune hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
x.mech: HCV replicates in oral keratinocytes and stimulates virus-specific CD8+ T-cells that cross-react with basal cell autoantigens.
x.lo: Identify Hepatitis C virus as an important association of lichen planus.
x.rev: Hepatitis C virus is strongly associated with lichen planus and warrants screening.

next.text: Review viral associations with dermatological diseases.

items.q: A 40-year-old woman complains of progressive scalp tenderness, burning, and patchy hair loss on the vertex of her scalp. Clinical inspection reveals perifollicular erythema, follicular hyperkeratosis, and smooth, shiny patches of complete hair loss where follicular ostia (openings) are entirely absent. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Lichen planopilaris is the follicular variant of lichen planus. It presents with perifollicular erythema, spinous hyperkeratosis, and progressive cicatricial (scarring) alopecia characterized by permanent destruction and loss of follicular ostia.
r: Correct: Loss of follicular ostia with perifollicular erythema indicates scarring alopecia from lichen planopilaris.
Alopecia areata is non-scarring; follicular ostia remain intact and exclamation mark hairs are present.
Androgenetic alopecia causes non-scarring progressive miniaturization of hair follicles without erythema or scarring.
Telogen effluvium is diffuse non-scarring hair shedding occurring 2-3 months after physiological stress.
items.kp: Lichen planopilaris is a follicular variant of lichen planus causing permanent scarring (cicatricial) alopecia with loss of follicular ostia.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for the management of lichen planus

x.key: Loss of follicular ostia with perifollicular inflammation indicates lichen planopilaris.

others.B: Alopecia areata is non-scarring with preserved ostia.

x.pearl: Once follicular ostia are destroyed, hair regrowth is impossible; prompt treatment with potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids is essential to halt progression.
x.clues: Scalp burning, vertex patches of hair loss, perifollicular erythema, absent follicular ostia.
x.ddx: Discoid lupus erythematosus, frontal fibrosing alopecia, pseudopelade of Brocq.
x.mech: T-cell mediated destruction of epithelial stem cells in the hair follicle bulge region leads to permanent fibrosis.
x.lo: Differentiate scarring from non-scarring alopecias and recognise lichen planopilaris.
x.rev: Lichen planopilaris causes irreversible cicatricial alopecia with destruction of follicular ostia.

items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with widespread, coalescent orange-red scaly plaques across his trunk, waxy orange-yellow thickening of the palms and soles ('PRP sandal'), and spiny follicular papules on the dorsal fingers. Notably, within extensive areas of erythema on his back, there are well-circumscribed islands of completely normal, unaffected skin. What is the diagnosis?
o: Exfoliative dermatitis due to drug eruption
items.exp: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a chronic papulosquamous disorder characterized by reddish-orange plaques, follicular plugging on the dorsal hands, waxy palmoplantar keratoderma, and pathognomonic 'islands of normal skin' within erythematous sheets.
r: Correct: Orange-red plaques, waxy keratoderma, and islands of normal skin are diagnostic of pityriasis rubra pilaris.
Plaque psoriasis features silvery-white scale, Auspitz sign, and does not show islands of normal skin within erythroderma.
Sézary syndrome is a leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma causing generalized erythroderma with pruritus and atypical Sézary cells in peripheral blood.
Exfoliative drug dermatitis lacks follicular plugging, waxy orange keratoderma, and islands of normal skin.
items.kp: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is characterized by orange-red plaques with 'islands of normal skin' and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines on pityriasis rubra pilaris

x.key: Orange-red plaques with islands of normal skin define pityriasis rubra pilaris.

others.B: Psoriasis lacks islands of normal skin and waxy orange palms.
others.D: Exfoliative drug eruption lacks PRP features.

x.pearl: Unlike psoriasis, PRP responds poorly to phototherapy and topical treatments, typically requiring systemic retinoids (e.g. acitretin) or biologics.
x.clues: Orange-red plaques, islands of normal skin, waxy palmoplantar keratoderma, dorsal hand follicular plugging.
x.ddx: Plaque psoriasis, Sézary syndrome, atopic erythroderma, toxic shock syndrome.
x.mech: Abnormal vitamin A metabolism and CARD14 mutations leading to keratinocyte hyperproliferation and follicular hyperkeratosis.
x.lo: Recognise the clinical hallmarks of pityriasis rubra pilaris.
x.rev: Pityriasis rubra pilaris presents with orange-red plaques, islands of normal skin, and waxy keratoderma.

next.text: Review erythrodermic conditions and differential diagnoses.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman in her 9th week of pregnancy develops typical pityriasis rosea with a herald patch and a secondary Christmas tree trunk rash. She is concerned about potential fetal risks. What viral reactivation has been implicated in pityriasis rosea pathogenesis that has been associated with premature delivery or fetal complications when acquired in early pregnancy?
items.exp: Pityriasis rosea is associated with systemic reactivation of Human Herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6 / HHV-7). When pityriasis rosea occurs in the first 15 weeks of gestation, higher viral loads of HHV-6 have been linked in some observational cohorts with an increased risk of miscarriage, warranting obstetric awareness and close fetal surveillance.
r: Correct: HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation is the recognized viral cause of pityriasis rosea.
VZV causes chickenpox and shingles, which have distinct vesicular lesions.
CMV causes congenital sensorineural deafness and periventricular calcifications, but not pityriasis rosea.
Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek) and fetal hydrops, not pityriasis rosea.
items.kp: Pityriasis rosea is driven by HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation; when occurring in early pregnancy, obstetric surveillance is warranted.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Information on pityriasis rosea in pregnancy

x.key: HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation drives pityriasis rosea and may carry early pregnancy risks.

others.D: Parvovirus B19 causes slapped cheek and hydrops.

x.pearl: Most pregnancies complicated by pityriasis rosea after 15 weeks proceed completely normally without adverse sequelae.
x.clues: Pityriasis rosea in first trimester of pregnancy, implicated virus.
x.mech: Reactivation of latent HHV-6/7 in peripheral mononuclear cells triggers reactive cutaneous exanthem via cytokine cascade.
x.lo: Identify the viral etiology of pityriasis rosea and clinical relevance in early pregnancy.
x.rev: HHV-6 and HHV-7 reactivation causes pityriasis rosea.

items.q: A 64-year-old man started on a thiazide diuretic and an ACE inhibitor for hypertension three months ago presents with pruritic, violaceous, polygonal scaly papules on his trunk and limbs. Skin biopsy reveals an interface dermatitis resembling lichen planus, but with prominent dermal eosinophils, focal parakeratosis, and deep perivascular infiltrates. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: A lichenoid drug eruption (drug-induced lichen planus) is triggered by medications such as thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, antimalarials, and gold. Histopathologically, the presence of eosinophils, focal parakeratosis, and deeper perivascular infiltrates distinguishes it from idiopathic lichen planus (which lacks parakeratosis and eosinophils).
r: Correct: Thiazide/ACE inhibitor trigger with eosinophils and parakeratosis defines a lichenoid drug eruption.
Idiopathic lichen planus lacks parakeratosis and typically has no tissue eosinophilia.
Lichen sclerosus causes ivory-white atrophic patches with follicular plugging, mainly anogenital.
Guttate psoriasis features neutrophil microabscesses (Munro) and follows streptococcal infections.
items.kp: Lichenoid drug eruptions are triggered by thiazides, ACE inhibitors, and beta-blockers, featuring eosinophils and parakeratosis on histology.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines on adverse cutaneous drug reactions

x.key: Thiazide/ACE-inhibitor trigger with eosinophils and parakeratosis indicates lichenoid drug eruption.

others.C: Lichen sclerosus causes ivory-white atrophic plaques.

x.pearl: Lichenoid drug eruptions often take several months to develop after drug initiation and several weeks to months to resolve after drug discontinuation.
x.clues: Thiazide and ACE inhibitor therapy, lichen planus-like rash, histology showing eosinophils and parakeratosis.
x.ddx: Idiopathic lichen planus, erythema multiforme, secondary syphilis.
x.mech: Drug haptens modify keratinocyte surface antigens, eliciting an aberrant cytotoxic T-cell response with secondary eosinophil recruitment.
x.lo: Differentiate a lichenoid drug eruption from idiopathic lichen planus.
x.rev: Lichenoid drug eruptions present with lichenoid lesions with histological eosinophils following drug exposure.
